title: ion multitenant edge quant warmup sensitivity 2028-10
content:
Executive summary:

This doc captures a focused benchmarking sweep we ran for Project Ion — a multitenant edge deployment hypothesis where small dedicated edge-GPU pools serve multiple low-throughput customers with heterogeneous prompt shapes. The goals were: measure cold-start and tail behavior when aggressive INT8/4-bit quantization is applied, evaluate proactive KV-cache warmup strategies across tenants, and estimate per-1M-token unit economics under realistic bursty traffic.

High-level takeaway:
- Quantization (4-bit hybrid with per-channel calibration) reduces steady-state cost by ~37% vs FP16 for the tested model, but increases cold-start p99 by ~290ms when caches are cold.
- Proactive warmup (prefill by replaying most-likely prefixes) reduces p99 cold-start penalty by ~65% while costing ~4% extra GPU-hours from background warming jobs — net positive for tenants with >2 QPS peaks.
- A conservative batching policy (max-latency window 40ms) preserves p50/p95 while enabling batching gains; larger windows improve throughput but substantially increase the p99 tail for small-burst workloads.

Test matrix and environment:
- Model: Open LLM-family-13B equivalent (causal decoder), served with Redwood runtime.
- Hardware: Edge racks with single A10G-like GPU (16 GB), NVMe local cache.
- Variants tested:
  A) FP16 baseline, no quantization, default cache warmup (none)
  B) 4-bit quantization (Hybrid-QLoRA-style), no warmup
  C) 4-bit quantization + proactive warmup agent (replay hot prefixes)
  D) 4-bit quantization + deferred batching (larger window)
- Workloads: mix of three tenant profiles (Retail-chat, Search-rewrite, Recommendations-short prompts). Overall synthetic QPS patterns: steady 0.5 QPS per tenant with microbursts to 8 QPS lasting 20s every 10 minutes.
- Measurement targets: p50/p95/p99 token-response latency for first-token and 1st-100-token streams, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, KV-cache hit rate, and estimated cost per 1M tokens (cloud unit cost mapped to edge pool).
- Duration: 72h continuous runs for each variant to capture diurnal and burst patterns.

Key metrics (median across tenants, with notes):
- Steady-state (post-warm, 1m after steady QPS):
  A) FP16: p50=28ms, p95=65ms, p99=120ms, throughput=4200 tokens/s, GPU util=78%, cost per 1M tokens = $38.6
  B) 4-bit (no warm): p50=30ms, p95=70ms, p99=140ms, throughput=5100 tokens/s, GPU util=64%, cost per 1M tokens = $24.4
  C) 4-bit + warmup: p50=29ms, p95=68ms, p99=125ms, throughput=5050 tokens/s, GPU util=66%, cost per 1M tokens = $25.4 (includes warmup GPU-hrs amortized)
  D) 4-bit + large batching: p50=45ms, p95=110ms, p99=260ms, throughput=6800 tokens/s, GPU util=88%, cost per 1M tokens = $19.1

- Cold-start / burst ingress (first 30s after idle):
  A) FP16: first-token p99 spike median = +320ms vs steady, cache-warm dynamics fast due to higher memory bandwidth.
  B) 4-bit (no warm): first-token p99 spike median = +610ms vs steady, many slow kernel falls when quant tables are cold and KV misses occur.
  C) 4-bit + warmup: first-token p99 spike median = +210ms vs steady (warmup removed majority of heavy tail).
  D) 4-bit + large batching: p99 spike = +880ms (batch windows amplify queueing).

Operational observations:
- KV-cache warmup method: we implemented a tenant-aware replay agent that consumes historical prompt prefixes (top 100 popular prefixes per tenant) and performs low-priority background inference to populate key/value caches and tokenizers. This agent should be implemented with strict CPU/GPU throttling and tenant rate limits to avoid interfering with live traffic.
- Warmup cost tradeoff: for an edge node serving 8 tenants, warmup agents consumed ~0.6 GPU-hours per evening warmup pass, which increases amortized cost by ~4% but reduces cold-start p99 penalty substantially. For tenants with <0.2 average QPS the ROI is marginal.
- Quantization fragility: 4-bit hybrid quant showed consistent throughput and minimal steady-state quality regressions on our eval prompts, but we saw occasional latency jitter caused by kernel-fallbacks when sequence length distribution deviated (very long tokens / long contexts). Fallback detection and automated temporary model-variant routing (to FP16) is necessary to maintain SLOs.
- Batching tradeoffs: increasing batching window delivered the best cost/throughput but degraded p99 heavily for bursty multitenant patterns. We recommend adaptive batch windows (cut to 10ms when measured queue >100ms) rather than static large windows.

Recommendations for Ion PoC next phase:
1) Roll C (4-bit + proactive warmup) into a limited customer pilot for tenants with predictable burst shapes. Document warmup schedule and tenant opt-in.
2) Implement runtime fallback policy: detect kernel-fallback events and automatically route those requests to FP16 variant for 30s with circuit-breaker backoff. Log events to tracing.
3) Add warmup simulator to Redwood console: allow customers to preview warmup cost vs expected p99 improvement for their request profiles.
4) Expose tenant-level warmup toggles and quota token for warmup windows; surface in Console and API (boolean + budget param).
5) For edge pools where GPU memory < 20GB, restrict aggressive quant to models with <8192 context lengths or ensure streaming chunking enabled.

Runbook snippets (for SRE/ops):
- Detecting cold-cache incidents: trace tag 'kv-miss-rate' > 70% for 30s and p99 > 500ms => trigger warmup-agent run for affected tenant set and escalate metrics to on-call.
- Emergency degrade: if p99 > 900ms for 60s and GPU util < 50% (indicates serialization/blocking), temporarily switch traffic to FP16 replica or route to regional Dedicated pool with fallback.
- Warmup safety: warmup jobs must be scheduled with niceness >= 20, GPU fractional slices and capped to 0.5 extra GPUs per edge rack to avoid noisy neighbor effects.

Open questions / further experiments:
- Warmup cadence optimization: we tried once-daily evening pass; would hourly micro-warmups keyed to tenant peak windows be more cost-effective? Need A/B test with two tenants.
- Dynamic quant switching: can we automatically re-quantize per-model on the edge node in low-traffic windows to reduce storage overhead without affecting runtime latency?
- Prefetch selection: our top-100-prefix heuristic worked well, but a sketch-based popularity estimator might further reduce warmup cost while preserving hit-rate.
- Cost amortization model: refine mapping from edge GPU-hours to per-1M-token cost using real customer bills (current numbers use proxy spot rates).

Appendix: quick commands and artifacts
- repro playbook: run-sweep.sh --variant=C --tenants=8 --duration=72h --burst-pattern=microburst-8qps-20s
- dashboards to view: Console > Pools > ion-edge-*-kv-heatmap, Traces > kv-miss-longtail, Billing > edge-billing/ion-pool.
- Related tickets and PRs: JIRA-ION-POC-7123 (warmup agent), github.com/redwood-inference/ion-poc#pr-184 (quant kernels instrumentation).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally experimental and contains rough cost proxies. Please check linked billing tickets before quoting prices externally. Looking for sign-off from Daniel (perf-validation) and SRE (Marcos) on warmup safety knobs.

End of report.
